decision.explanation: Reversing orientation changes the sign: the integrals over C₁ and C₂ are 1 and −4, respectively. Adding them gives the integral over C as 1−4=−3.

after.name: Question 1
after.worked_solution:
Let $C={C}_{1}\cup {C}_{2}$ be a piecewise smooth path in the $xy$-plane, and let $-C$ be the curve consisting of the same points as $C$ but with the opposite orientation. 

For line integrals with respect to $x,$ we have the following properties:

- ${\int }_{-C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x=-{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x$

- ${\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x={\int }_{{C}_{1}}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{{C}_{2}}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x$

In our case, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{{C}_{1}}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{{C}_{2}}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x \\  & =-{\int }_{-{C}_{1}}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x-{\int }_{-{C}_{2}}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x \\  & =-(-1)-4 \\  & =-3.\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: Reversing orientation gives the integral over C as −9. Additivity gives −9 = −3 + the integral over C₂, so the integral over C₂ is −6. Reversing C₂ therefore gives 6.

after.name: Question 2
after.worked_solution:
Let $C={C}_{1}\cup {C}_{2}$ be a piecewise smooth path in the $xy$-plane, and let $-C$ be the curve consisting of the same points as $C$ but with the opposite orientation. 

For line integrals with respect to $y,$ we have the following properties:

- ${\int }_{-C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y=-{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y$

- ${\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y={\int }_{{C}_{1}}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y+{\int }_{{C}_{2}}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y$

In our case, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y & ={\int }_{{C}_{1}}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y+{\int }_{{C}_{2}}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y \\ -{\int }_{-C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y & =-3-{\int }_{-{C}_{2}}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y \\ -9 & =-3-{\int }_{-{C}_{2}}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y \\ -6 & =-{\int }_{-{C}_{2}}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{\int }_{-{C}_{2}}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y=6.
$$

after.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14079767/assets/9c42d875a65a6b54ad7769180f5ec2e831772ad44a89ec913951da40c6d90514.png)

Calculate ${\int }_{C}\,\text{d}y,$ where $C$ is the path along the line segment between the points $(-3,0)$ to the point $(0,2),$ as shown above.
after.worked_solution:
The line integral of unity with respect to $y$ along a path $C$ is equal to the net change in $y$ between the terminal and initial points:

$$
{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}y={y}_{2}-{y}_{1},
$$

where ${y}_{2}$ is the $y$-coordinate of the terminal point, and ${y}_{1}$ is the $y$-coordinate of the initial point.

In our case, ${y}_{2}=2$ and ${y}_{1}=0.$ Therefore,

$$
{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}y={y}_{2}-{y}_{1}=2-0=2.
$$

Calculate ${∮}_{C}\,\text{d}y,$ where $C$ is the closed path along the rectangle, traversed once in the counterclockwise direction, as shown above.
after.worked_solution:
The line integral of unity with respect to $y$ along a path $C$ is equal to the net change in $y$ between the terminal and initial points:

$$
{∮}_{C}\,\text{d}y={y}_{2}-{y}_{1},
$$

where ${y}_{2}$ is the $y$-coordinate of the terminal point, and ${y}_{1}$ is the $y$-coordinate of the initial point.

In our case, the initial and terminal points are the same (since the path is closed and is traversed only once). Therefore, ${y}_{1}={y}_{2},$ and we have

$$
{∮}_{C}\,\text{d}y=0.
$$
